newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela nets $1.5 billion on 12 oil contracts.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela nets $1.5 billion on 12 oil contracts.

text.p: Private companies have paid $1.5 billion for 12 contracts to exploit ageing Venezuelan oilfields and many of the biggest companies have yet to hit the jackpot in Venezuela's third day of operating contract sales.

On Wednesday, it was companies with existing ties to Venezuela's oil industry that won contracts, with China's National Petroleum Corp (CNPC) netting a second contract, this time in the east of the country.
The size of the bids shocked some delegates at the five-day bidding round, particularly when international oil companies like British Petroleum were outbid by state enterprises.

"Some of the highest bids reflect companies' strategy to get into the Venezuelan oil market," said Petroconsultants analyst Patricia Sosa. "BP has business all over the world, including Venezuela, so it wasn't worth them risking a larger bid, while for CNPC, the idea of going abroad is a new venture, so their assessment was totally different."

CNPC brought its bid total to $358 million with its $241 million offer for the Caracoles field in eastern Venezuela. CNPC representative Wang Shaoxian said this was only part of China's growing presence in the country and she was also looking at investing in Venezuela's huge extra-heavy crude reserves in the Orinoco Oil Belt.
Phillips Petroleum Co, a partner in one of five existing Orinoco crude projects, won its first operating contract in the Ambrosio field in western Venezuela for $31 million.
Only two companies offered bids for this field, in what Phillips described as difficult geology, but the company hoped to get 25,000 barrels per day (bpd) production within six years.
Phillips global ventures manager Paul Appel said the company was also in preliminary talks about a petrochemical venture in Venezuela.
A consortium comprising Statoil, Chevron Corp, ARCO and Phillips paid the day's top price of $251 million for the LL652 contract, which Statoil described as the prize of the round.
They expected to pump over 100,000 bpd from the field within six years on investments of $1 billion to $1.5 billion over the 20 year life of the contract.

Statoil and ARCO are also partners in two separate Orinoco heavy crude projects and Chevron is operating Venezuela's Boscan field, the most prolific of the fields offered in previous operating rounds.

Oil giant Shell and Exxon have yet to bid for fields in this round, but Luis Giusti, president of state owned Petroelos de Venezuela (PDVSA), noted that some of the biggest fields -- Dacion and Boqueron -- are yet to come.
The Cretacico Sur field, also on the block on Wednesday, received no bids, however.
PDVSA exploration chief Juan Szabo said the high acid content, complicated geology and lack of infrastructure near this field could explain the lack of interest.

"Maybe this contract doesn't really suit an area with fractured deposits and very little exploration activity," a consultant attending the round said. "The Cretacico Sur area is not so much a reactivation contract as an exploration contract."
PDVSA is hoping to attract foreign oil companies to participate in its nationalised oil industry as part of its ambitious plan to double output in ten years.

Although the operating contracts are complicated, participants say they offer companies the chance to recoup their investment by raising production and then get 30 percent of the profits from any additional output, up to a pre-set ceiling.
